content: 1. Mobile phone technology has been explored as a tool to enhance the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV in Nyanza, Kenya. A qualitative study published in BMC Public Health in 2013 (Volume 13, Article 1131) examined its potential impact. 2. In India, mobile phones have been identified as a promising solution to address healthcare challenges in rural areas. This was discussed in a 2012 article in the Journal of Health Informatics in Developing Countries (Volume 6, Issue 1). 3. A cluster-randomized controlled trial conducted in Zanzibar investigated the use of mobile phones as a health communication tool to improve skilled attendance during childbirth. The findings were published in BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology in 2012 (Volume 119, Issue 10, Pages 1256–1264). 4. The Text4Diet study, a randomized controlled trial, evaluated the effectiveness of text messaging in promoting weight loss behaviors. The results were published in Preventive Medicine in 2012 (Volume 55, Issue 5, Pages 412–417). 5. A randomized controlled trial assessed the use of text messaging to improve attendance at post-operative clinic visits following adult male circumcision for HIV prevention. The study, published in PLoS One in 2012 (Volume 7, Issue 9, Article e43832), demonstrated the potential of this intervention. 6. A study in Tanzania evaluated the feasibility, reach, and potential impact of a text message-based family planning information service. The findings were published in Contraception in 2013 (Volume 87, Issue 2, Pages 251–256). 7. A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examined the design of text message interventions to promote adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART). The results were published in PLoS One in 2014 (Volume 9, Issue 2, Article e88166). 8. A study investigated the effect of daily text messages on the continuation of oral contraceptives. The findings were published in Obstetrics & Gynecology in 2012 (Volume 119, Issue 1, Pages 14–20). 9. In Tanzania, electronic technology was used to improve clinical care by assessing and classifying sick children according to the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) protocol. The results of this before-and-after cluster trial were published in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making in 2013 (Volume 13, Article 1). 10. In Liberia, cell phones were utilized to collect pregnancy data from remote areas. This study was published in the Journal of Nursing Scholarship in 2012 (Volume 44, Issue 3, Pages 294–301). 11. The WelTel Kenya1 trial, a randomized study, evaluated the effects of mobile phone short message service (SMS) on adherence to antiretroviral treatment in Kenya. The results were published in The Lancet in 2010 (Volume 376, Issue 9755, Pages 1838–1845). 12. A study in Ciudad Juárez used an intersectionality approach to understand the experiences of parents raising children in a violent context. The findings were published in Women’s Studies International Forum in 2013 (Volume 40, Pages 10–22). 13. The TREND statement was developed to improve the reporting quality of non-randomized evaluations of behavioral and public health interventions. This was published in the American Journal of Public Health in 2004 (Volume 94, Issue 3, Pages 361–366). 14. The STROBE statement provides guidelines for reporting observational studies in epidemiology. These guidelines were published in Preventive Medicine in 2007 (Volume 45, Issue 4, Pages 247–251). 15. The STARD initiative outlines guidelines for reporting diagnostic test accuracy studies. This was discussed in the Journal of Personality Assessment in 2010 (Volume 81, Issue 3, Pages 191–193). 16. The CONSORT 2010 statement provides updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomized trials. This was published in BMC Medicine in 2010 (Volume 8, Article 32). 17. The COREQ checklist, a 32-item guideline for reporting qualitative research involving interviews and focus groups, was published in the International Journal for Quality in Health Care in 2007 (Volume 19, Issue 6, Pages 349–357). 18. The SQUIRE project developed publication guidelines for quality improvement in healthcare. This was discussed in Quality and Safety in Health Care in 2008 (Volume 17, Supplement 1, Pages i3–i9). 19. The MHEALTH Evidence Reporting and Assessment (MERA) checklist provides a framework for monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions. It includes definitions of key terms such as analytic studies, benchmarks, claims, and conceptual frameworks. 20. Analytic studies aim to quantify the relationship between an intervention and its outcomes, often to demonstrate causality. These studies are categorized as experimental or observational. 21. Digital health refers to the use of digital, mobile, and wireless technologies to achieve health objectives. It encompasses mHealth and eHealth applications. 22. Effectiveness refers to the ability of a digital health intervention to achieve intended results in real-world settings, while efficacy pertains to controlled research environments. 23. Evaluation involves systematically assessing an intervention’s objectives, efficiency, effectiveness, impact, and sustainability. This includes analyzing user interactions and changes attributable to the intervention. 24. Experimental studies, such as randomized controlled trials (RCTs), assess the effects of an intervention on specific outcomes. 25. Feasibility measures whether a digital health system can function as intended in a given context, while fidelity assesses whether the intervention is delivered as planned. 26. Focus group discussions (FGDs) and in-depth interviews (IDIs) are qualitative research methods used to gather opinions, perspectives, and experiences from individuals or groups. 27. Indicators are quantitative or qualitative variables used to measure achievement or assess performance related to an intervention. 28. Inputs refer to the resources—financial, human, material, or intellectual—used to develop and implement an intervention. 29. Logical frameworks or logic models summarize a project’s objectives, assumptions, and expected causal links between inputs, processes, outputs, outcomes, and impacts. 30. Mobile health (mHealth) involves using mobile and wireless technologies to support health objectives, such as delivering antenatal care messages to pregnant women. 31. Monitoring burden refers to the effort and resources required to monitor an intervention, influenced by factors such as maturity, scale, and data volume. 32. Observational studies assess relationships between exposures and outcomes without intervention by the investigator. 33. Outcomes represent intermediate changes resulting from inputs and processes, while outputs are the direct deliverables of intervention activities. 34. Participatory action research (PAR) emphasizes the role of participants in all aspects of research and implementation, using quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods. 35. Performance measures how well an intervention or implementation team meets specific criteria, standards, or goals. 36. Pilot studies are small-scale deployments used to assess feasibility, acceptability, and cost, often informing decisions about scaling up. 37. Probability sampling involves random selection, giving all individuals in a population an equal chance of being included in a survey. 38. Processes refer to the activities undertaken to deliver an intervention, such as training, partnership meetings, and system updates. 39. Process monitoring involves continuously collecting and analyzing data to compare implementation progress against expected results. 40. Quality measures the excellence, value, and ability of a digital health intervention to meet or exceed expectations, viewed from both user and content perspectives. 41. Quality assurance (QA) test cases describe expected functionality and steps to perform specific system functions, ensuring alignment with use cases and system requirements. 42. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assess the efficacy or effectiveness of an intervention by comparing outcomes between intervention and control groups, with random allocation. 43. A results framework graphically represents a strategy to achieve specific objectives, grounded in cause-and-effect logic.
